opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a hugely promising direction, and in some ways it's surprising it took the field this long to lean into it.

The basic intuition is simple: right now, when you ask a model a question, it's doing a roughly fixed amount of computation per token, whether you asked it "what's two plus two" or something that would take a human expert a week. That's obviously not how intelligence should work. Some problems deserve a lot more thought than others. So if you can let the model think longer, explore multiple approaches, check its own work, and backtrack when it's wrong, you can get a lot more capability out of the same underlying model.

And the economics are kind of striking. Running these models is incredibly cheap per operation compared to almost anything else. A forward pass costs a tiny fraction of a cent per token. If you compare that to what it costs to pay a person to think about a problem, or even to buy a paperback book, the compute is basically free. So there's an enormous amount of headroom. If spending a hundred times or a thousand times more compute on a hard question gets you a meaningfully better answer, that's a great trade for a lot of applications: coding, math, science, anything where being right matters a lot.

The open question is how well it scales and on which kinds of problems. It works really nicely where you can verify answers, like math or code where you can run tests. It's harder in fuzzier domains where it's not obvious what "better" means. But I don't think that's a fundamental wall. It's more a matter of research.

So I see it as complementary to scaling up training, not a replacement. You want smarter base models, and you want them to be able to use more thinking when the problem calls for it. Both of those multiply together, and I think we're still pretty early on the inference side.

r001.rationale: The response says inference operations are extremely cheap compared with paying a person to think, leaving substantial headroom to spend more compute for better answers.

r002.rationale: It describes greater capability from letting models think longer and explicitly discusses how well capability scales as inference compute increases.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise whether inference-time scaling could reach artificial general intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most important levers we have, and honestly it's a little embarrassing that we didn't lean into it harder sooner.

Here's the way I think about it. If you look at where the compute goes today, training is enormous but it's amortized. You spend it once and then you serve the model to hundreds of millions of people. Inference, on the other hand, is per-query, and for most queries we spend an absurdly small amount. A model answers a hard math problem or a nuanced question about someone's life with a few hundred thousand floating point operations per token, and it does it in a fraction of a second. If you asked a human to do that with no time to think, they'd do terribly too. So the question is really, what happens when you let the system think?

And what we've seen is that it works. Chain of thought, search over reasoning paths, verifiers, sampling many candidates and picking the best, agents that iterate and check their own work: all of these are ways of converting more inference compute into better answers. The nice thing is that the curves look really favorable. Going from one sample to a thousand samples on a hard problem is a few orders of magnitude of compute, but that's often cheaper than training a model that would get it right in one shot. And the cost of inference is on a steep downward slope, so what looks expensive now looks cheap in a couple of years.

There are a few things I'd flag, though. First, it's not free lunch across the board. It helps most on problems where you can verify or at least evaluate the answer, like code, math, planning, anything with a feedback signal. It helps less when the problem is "write me something tasteful," because you don't have a great way to tell the good samples from the bad ones. Second, the real win is when training and inference-time compute reinforce each other. You use the expensive, slow, thinking-hard version of the model to generate better data, you train the fast version on that, and now the fast version's baseline is higher and the thinking version starts from a better place. That loop is the thing I'm most excited about.

And third, there's a systems question that people underrate. Spending more compute at inference means you need hardware and serving stacks that are good at it: long contexts, lots of parallel samples, efficient batching across users who are all thinking at once. A lot of my career has been about making the numbers go fast, and I think inference-time scaling is going to put as much pressure on the engineering as it does on the research.

So my overall assessment is that it's a huge deal, probably as big a story as scaling pretraining was, and we're still early. The models are already smart enough that giving them room to think changes what they can do. We just have to build the systems to let them.

r001.rationale: The response calls inference compute per-query “absurdly small” and says it can be cheaper than training, but it never compares that cost with human labor or identifies that comparison as economic room to spend more.

r002.rationale: It says the curves are favorable and describes how spending more inference compute—such as sampling many candidates—can improve answers.

r003.rationale: It calls inference-time scaling a huge deal and says the field is early, but does not raise whether it can reach artificial general intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there. If you ask a person a hard question, you generally get a better answer if you give them some time to think. We’d like the same thing to be true of these systems: spend more computation on a particular problem and get a better answer.

The question is how to use that computation productively. You can generate multiple candidate solutions, check them, revise them, or break the problem into smaller pieces. That’s particularly promising in domains where you can verify the answer, like programming or mathematics. If you can tell whether a solution works, searching for one becomes much more useful.

But simply making a model produce more text doesn’t necessarily make it smarter. You need it to learn how to make progress with that extra computation. So I think there’s a big opportunity, and training and inference compute are complementary: you spend compute during training to teach the system how to use its thinking time effectively.

r001.rationale: The response sees potential in spending more inference compute, but does not mention inference’s low cost relative to human labor or the resulting economic room to spend more.

r002.rationale: It says more computation could produce a better answer, but does not predict a scaling curve in capability as inference-time compute increases.

r003.rationale: The response does not address whether inference-time scaling could reach artificial general intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there. If you ask a model to answer immediately, you’re putting a pretty hard limit on how much computation it can do. For a difficult problem, you’d like it to be able to work for a while—try different approaches, check its work, and revise the answer.

The tricky part is making that extra computation useful. You don’t necessarily get a better answer just by generating more tokens. You need to train the system to use that time effectively, and ideally to recognize when it has made progress and when it’s going in circles.

It’s particularly promising for problems where checking an answer is easier than finding one, like a lot of math and programming tasks. You can generate candidates and test them. For more open-ended questions, figuring out which answer is better is itself a difficult problem.

So I’d expect inference compute to become another important axis of scaling, alongside training compute. And you’d want to allocate it dynamically: very little for an easy question, much more for something where the additional thinking is valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the potential value of extra inference compute but does not mention its low cost relative to human labor or the resulting economic room to spend more.

r002.rationale: It predicts inference compute will become another scaling axis and describes allocating more compute to improve answers on harder problems.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise whether inference-time scaling could reach artificial general intelligence.
